<reason>A genuinely close, high-quality debate. PRO built a clean weighing frame (default-on costs 30 seconds, default-off costs a bank statement) and skillfully exploited CON's deliberate concession that minors don't fund free access, which drained the motion's "even if" clause of cost. But CON absorbed that concession as a proportionality bar and, in the later rounds, landed two rebuttals PRO never neutralized: (1) the casino disanalogy—slot machines are age-gated because money comes back out, not because of anticipation psychology—which undercut PRO's slot-machine framing and PRO's own "we age-gate casinos, not claw machines" answer; and (2) the closing turn that a parent-authenticated $20 bankroll empties just like a claw machine's coin pocket, the very case PRO had said falls outside regulation under its own "delivery capacity" line. PRO's best remaining ground—odds display, pull counts, and cooling-off living inside the game after the PIN—was a real answer to CON's Q1, and the "lock on the front door / slot machine in the bedroom" image was memorable, but PRO spoke before CON's closing and could not respond to the bankroll point, and PRO never addressed CON's identity-infrastructure cost claim about "verified adult authorization." CON's narrowing of the clash to "existing default authentication vs. a new identity-verified mechanic regime" was slightly cleaner for a reader to decide. Two of PRO's turns were clipped versus one of CON's, a minor execution cost. Razor-thin edge to CON.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's A2 answer in Rebuttal 2—"the feature a casino has that a loot system lacks is simple: money comes back out"—directly answered PRO's pressure question, distinguished gambling law's actual trigger from reward psychology, and explained why claw machines and card packs go unregulated. PRO never rebutted it, and CON's closing extended it into the "claw machine with a twenty-dollar coin pocket" turn against PRO's own delivery-capacity standard.</best_rebuttal>
